newsitem.title: UK: EMU bond plays still bullish after Italy ERM move.
newsitem.headline: EMU bond plays still bullish after Italy ERM move.

text.p: Europe's high-yielding bonds have moved closer to German government bonds all year and Italy's return to Europe's currency grid ultimately will benefit such EMU-oriented strategies, analysts said on Monday.
Yield convergence -- betting that the differences between bond yields will narrow as European economic and monetary union (EMU) approaches -- has proved the most lucrative bond strategy in 1996.
After a dose of profit-taking, analysts said the trend should resume.
"The whole thing has got a bit of a 'Buy on the rumour, sell on the fact' feel to it," said Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at Barclays de Zoete Wedd in London.
"As we get closer and closer to year-end a number of players have done well on this trade (and will want to sell)," she said.

Adrian Owens, European economist at Bank Julius Baer in London, agreed there was likely to be some profit-taking, but added that Italy's re-entry into the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) showed the convergence strategy remained on track.
Italy's weekend move back into the currency grid that sets fluctuation bands for member currencies, caps a year of fast-moving EMU developments.
As markets became convinced that Europe's leaders had the political will to push EMU through, investors swooped in on the highest-yielding bonds in Europe, such as Italian BTPs.

At the start of the year, 10-year BTPs were yielding 4.75 percentage points points more than German government bonds, or Bunds, which are the market benchmark. They currently yield just 1.7 points more than Bunds.
After pulling out of the ERM in 1992 amid rampant mark strength, the lira went into freefall before finally regaining its poise in the past couple of years.
Late on Sunday, European Union (EU) finance ministers and central bank governors agreed to let the lira rejoin the ERM at a central rate of 990 lire to the mark.
One of the criteria for monetary union is that long-term interest rates in Europe converge, with no member having rates more than two percentage points above the best three members.
"This should ensure that the impetus continues. The mere fact that Italy has taken a further step forward towards EMU will have a knock-on effect for other markets," said Owens.

Spain and Sweden have been the other two main beneficiaries of EMU optimism. Spanish 10-year Bonos narrowed the gap against Bunds to a record low of 1.28 percentage points in early European trade. Swedish bonds were yielding 1.39 points over Bunds.
Reed said bond investors for the time being were likely to use this as an opportunity to get out of BTPs and into markets such as British government securities, or gilts.

Gilts have lagged other markets this year amid uncertainty over whether Britain would ever embrace EMU like other European nations. The spread of gilt to Bunds exceeded the BTP/Bund gap for the first time recently.
The 10-year gilt spread was at 1.79 percentage points on Monday.
"We'll probably see spreads widening out. You wouldn't like to sell them too hard though," Reed said.
Italian bonds still had a number of things going for them, including falling inflation and the likelihood of further interest rate cuts, analysts said.
"The mood is still bullish, said Alfredo Granata, analyst at Banca di Roma in Rome.
Granata said the spread against Bunds would continue to narrow in line with the inflation diffential between the two countries.
Owens at Bank Julius Baer pointed to a year-end target of 1.5 percentage points.

Reed said the rate at which the lira re-entered the ERM would not prevent the Italian authorities cutting interest rates while the amount that currencies are allowed to fluctuate within the currency grid remained at 15 percent.
